title: Safeguarding children
blurb: The four categories of abuse, signs the dental team may see, dental neglect, and exactly who you tell when you're worried about a child.
question: A 6-year-old has bruising on both cheeks and behind one ear. Her father says she fell off her bike. She has several untreated decayed teeth and was not brought to her last three appointments. What should concern you, and what should you do next?

teach.body: Safeguarding means protecting children (anyone under 18) from abuse and neglect, preventing harm to their health or development, and making sure they grow up with safe, effective care. Child protection is the part of safeguarding that acts when a child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm. The dental team sees children regularly, often with their families, so you are well placed to notice when something isn't right. The GDC expects every registrant to raise concerns when a child may be at risk.

teach.h: The four categories of child abuse

children.label: Neglect
children.sub: Persistent failure to meet basic needs

teach.caption: These are the categories used in UK child protection guidance. A child may suffer more than one kind.

teach.h: Signs the dental team may notice
head: Type
Possible signs
rows: Bruises on cheeks, ears or neck; bite marks; burns; torn frenum in a baby; story doesn't fit the injury
Withdrawn, very anxious, 'frozen watchfulness', desperate to please
Unexplained oral injuries or infections; age-inappropriate behaviour
Untreated decay causing pain; repeatedly not brought; poor hygiene; hungry or unkempt
teach.caption: Injuries to the head, face and mouth are common in physical abuse, so the dental team may be the first to see them. One sign alone doesn't prove abuse: it's a reason to share a concern.

teach.body: Dental neglect is the persistent failure to meet a child's basic oral health needs, in a way likely to seriously harm their oral or general health or development. A single cavity is not neglect. It becomes a concern when untreated disease causes pain, infection or loss of sleep, and parents don't act despite support. Say a child 'was not brought' rather than 'did not attend': children depend on adults to get them to appointments.

teach.h: A staged approach to dental neglect
items: Preventive dental team management: explain the problem to the parents, offer support and a clear plan, record it, and keep a close eye on attendance.
Preventive multi-agency management: if there's no improvement, liaise with others who know the family, such as the health visitor, school nurse or GP.
Child protection referral: if there is still no improvement, or there are other concerns, refer through the safeguarding lead to children's social care.

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Facts, exact words, date, time, signed

steps.label: Refer
steps.sub: To children's social care, as agreed

steps.label: Follow up
steps.sub: Check the referral was received and acted on

teach.caption: This mirrors the approach taught in 'Child Protection and the Dental Team'. You don't decide whether abuse happened: you share the concern.

teach.h: If a child tells you something
teach.body: Stay calm and listen. Take it seriously and let them talk. Don't ask leading questions, and never promise to keep it secret: explain you'll need to tell someone who can help. Write down their exact words as soon as possible, with the date and time, and tell the safeguarding lead the same day. A child's welfare comes before confidentiality, so sharing information to protect a child is the right thing to do.

teach.caption: Every practice should have a named safeguarding lead and local referral numbers on display. Known FGM in a girl under 18 must be reported to the police by the registered professional (England and Wales).

teach.text: Don't investigate, confront the parent, or wait for proof. And don't just make a private note 'in case it happens again'. Follow the practice safeguarding procedure and tell the safeguarding lead.

items: Four categories: physical, emotional, sexual, neglect.
Watch for facial, ear and neck bruising, stories that don't fit, untreated pain, and children repeatedly not brought.
Dental neglect is persistent; use a staged approach: dental team, multi-agency, then child protection referral.
Observe, record, communicate, refer, follow up.
Immediate danger: 999. Otherwise: safeguarding lead, same day.
Never promise a child secrecy; their welfare outweighs confidentiality.

summary: You can now name the four categories of child abuse, recognise signs the dental team may see, explain dental neglect and the staged response to it, and follow the right route to raise a concern about a child.

A.q: You become aware that a child attending the practice may be at risk of harm. What should you do?
options: Discuss it with the child's parent first
Keep a private note in case it recurs
Raise it with the practice safeguarding lead
Wait until you are certain abuse is happening
A.why: Concerns about a child are raised through the practice safeguarding procedure and the safeguarding lead, without delay.

whyNot.0: Raising it with the parent could put the child at greater risk.
whyNot.1: A private note means nobody acts on the concern.
whyNot.3: You don't need proof; you need to share a reasonable concern.

A.q: Which of these is one of the four recognised categories of child abuse?
options: Financial
Organisational
Discriminatory
Neglect
A.why: The four categories for children are physical, emotional, sexual abuse and neglect.

whyNot.0: Financial abuse is a category used for adults at risk.
whyNot.1: Organisational abuse is listed in adult safeguarding guidance.
whyNot.2: Discriminatory abuse is listed in adult safeguarding guidance.

A.q: A child tells you a family member hurts her, then asks you to keep it a secret. What should you say?
options: 'I promise I won't tell anyone.'
'Are you sure? That's a serious thing to say.'
'I'll need to tell someone who can help you.'
'Let's ask your mum about it together.'
A.why: Never promise secrecy. Be honest that you must share it with someone who can help, then tell the safeguarding lead.

whyNot.0: You can't keep this promise, and breaking it later damages trust.
whyNot.1: Questioning whether she's telling the truth can stop her talking.
whyNot.3: Involving the family could put the child at further risk.

B.q: Which injury pattern on a child should raise the most concern?
options: Grazed knees after a fall in the park
Bruising on the shins of an active child
Bruising to both ears and the neck
A bruised forehead in a toddler learning to walk
B.why: Bruising to soft, protected areas such as the ears and neck is rarely accidental and should raise concern.

whyNot.0: Grazed knees are typical accidental injuries.
whyNot.1: Shins are a common site of accidental bruising in active children.
whyNot.3: Toddlers often bump bony areas like the forehead when learning to walk.

B.q: A child with toothache has not been brought to four appointments, and the parents have not acted despite support. This may indicate:
options: Dental neglect
Emotional abuse
Dental anxiety only
Normal childhood caries
B.why: Persistent failure to meet a child's basic oral health needs, despite support, may be dental neglect.

whyNot.1: Emotional abuse involves ill-treatment like threats or rejection, not missed care.
whyNot.2: Anxiety doesn't explain parents' failure to act on pain despite support.
whyNot.3: Caries alone isn't neglect, but untreated pain plus repeated missed care is a concern.

B.q: What should you write in the record after a child discloses abuse?
options: A summary of what you think really happened
Their exact words, with date and time
Only your opinion of the parents
Nothing until social care asks
B.why: Record the facts and the child's exact words, dated, timed and signed. Accurate records support any referral.

whyNot.0: Your interpretation can distort what was said.
whyNot.2: Opinions without facts are not helpful and may be unfair.
whyNot.3: Records must be made promptly, not on request.

C.q: A child at the practice appears to be in immediate danger. Who should be contacted?
options: The child's school
The GDC
The police on 999
The practice owner by email
C.why: If a child is in immediate danger, call 999. The safeguarding lead should also be informed.

whyNot.0: The school may need to know later, but it can't respond to immediate danger.
whyNot.1: The GDC regulates professionals; it doesn't respond to child protection emergencies.
whyNot.3: Email is far too slow when a child is in danger.

C.q: Why should the practice record 'was not brought' rather than 'did not attend' for a child?
options: It is shorter to write in the notes
Children rely on adults to bring them
It removes the need for follow-up
It is required for NHS fee claims
C.why: Children can't attend on their own. 'Was not brought' keeps the focus on whether the child's needs are being met.

whyNot.2: Missed appointments still need follow-up, and may be a safeguarding sign.
whyNot.3: It's a safeguarding approach, not a fee rule.

C.q: In the staged approach to dental neglect, what comes BEFORE a child protection referral (unless there are other concerns)?
options: Discharging the child and family from the practice list
Waiting a full year to see whether things improve
Telling the child off for not brushing
Preventive work with the family and other agencies
C.why: The staged approach starts with preventive dental team support, then multi-agency work, then referral if there's no improvement.

whyNot.0: Discharging a child removes support and can hide neglect.
whyNot.1: Delaying a year could leave the child in pain.
whyNot.2: The child is not responsible; the adults are.

reteach.title: You're a smoke alarm, not a firefighter
reteach.question: A smoke alarm doesn't put out fires or decide what caused them. It just sounds early so the right people can act. How is that your role in safeguarding?

blocks.body: Your job is to notice the 'smoke': a bruise that doesn't fit the story, a child who flinches, toothache that's been ignored for months. Then you record what you saw and heard, and pass it to the safeguarding lead, who works with children's social care. You don't investigate or confront anyone, any more than a smoke alarm climbs a ladder. If the fire is already burning (immediate danger), you call 999.

blocks.text: You don't need proof. A reasonable concern is enough to share.

explain.body: Physical, emotional, sexual and neglect. Watch for injuries in protected areas (ears, neck, cheeks), explanations that don't fit, fearful or withdrawn behaviour, and untreated pain.

test.q: A child seems watchful, still and fearful, and flinches when an adult moves near. This behaviour is most associated with:
options: Normal shyness
Dental anxiety only
Possible abuse
Tiredness after school
test.why: 'Frozen watchfulness' and flinching are recognised warning signs of possible abuse and should be shared as a concern.

whyNot.0: Shy children don't usually flinch at adult movement.
whyNot.1: Dental anxiety doesn't usually cause flinching at ordinary adult movement.

explain.body: Persistent failure to meet a child's basic oral health needs, likely to cause serious harm. Respond in stages: dental team support, then multi-agency work, then a child protection referral if there's no improvement.

test.q: Which situation best fits dental neglect?
options: One small cavity found at a check-up
Repeated untreated pain despite support
A child who dislikes the taste of toothpaste
A missed appointment due to illness
test.why: Neglect is persistent: untreated pain and infection with no action despite help being offered.

whyNot.0: A single cavity is common and isn't neglect.
whyNot.3: One explained missed appointment isn't persistent failure.

explain.body: Listen calmly, don't ask leading questions, never promise secrecy, record the exact words with date and time, and tell the safeguarding lead the same day.

test.q: When a child starts to disclose abuse, which response is best?
options: Ask detailed questions about what happened
Promise you'll keep it between you
Tell them they must be mistaken
Listen calmly and let them talk
test.why: Listening calmly without leading questions lets the child speak and keeps their account accurate.

whyNot.0: Detailed questioning is for trained investigators and can affect evidence.
whyNot.2: Disbelief may stop the child ever telling again.

explain.body: Immediate danger: 999. Otherwise the practice safeguarding lead, the same day, who refers to children's social care. If the lead isn't available, contact children's social care directly using the local numbers.

test.q: Who is usually the first person a dental nurse should go to with a non-urgent safeguarding concern?
options: The practice safeguarding lead
The child's GP
The local newspaper
The GDC
test.why: The practice safeguarding lead takes concerns forward and makes referrals to children's social care.

whyNot.1: The GP may be involved later, but the practice route starts with the lead.
whyNot.2: Publicising a concern breaches confidentiality and could harm the child.
whyNot.3: The GDC regulates professionals; it doesn't take child referrals.
